speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I beg to move:
That the recommendation of His Honour the Speaker, laid upon the table of the House on 15th instant, respecting' the appointment of Mr. Arthur Beauchesne, B.A., K.C., to the position of Clerk Assistant of the House of Commons, be concurred in.	[DOT]

Mr. Beauchesne has been an officer of the Department of Justice, and it is proposed that he be transferred in this way, and at the same salary.

I have no objection to the appointment of Mr. Beauchesne; I think he is well qualified for the position; but I am sorry that the system of promotion has not been followed, and that some official of the House was not promoted to this position. The system of promotion should be followed as much as possible. With regard to his predecessor, the late Mr. Laplante, I know that the House realizes fully the value of his services. Perhaps I am in a position to appreciate them more than any other member of the House, by reason of the fact that. I was Deputy Speaker, and afterwards Speaker, for a considerable time. I would suggest to the Prime Minister whether, in view of the unfortunate circumstances of his death, it would not be possible to do something for Mr. Laplante's widow. I understand that she is only to receive, two months' salary as a gratuity. I hope the Prime Minister1 will see his way to deal with the matter, and try to secure some suitable provision for the widow.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The appointment of Mr. Beauchesne does not involve promotion, strictly speaking, from amongst the staff of the House of Commons; but it is promotion, although at the same salary, in the Civil Service itself. I entirely agree with what my hon. friend has said with regard to the great value of the late Mr. Laplante's services. I always found him a most capable and most faithful officer, and, as I took occasion to say on a previous occasion, I fully realize that his death , is a great loss to this House.
With regard to what my hon. friend has suggested, respecting some assistance to his family, I have not had that matter under consideration. There is a subJCommittee of Council, convened I think by the Minister of Justice, to whom such matters are referred, and I shall be very glad indeed to place the suggestion of my hon. friend before that committee with the view of giving it the most favourable consideration possible, having regard to the public interest, and to the precedents generally followed in such matters.
Motion agreed to.

On the Orders of the Day:

I would ask my hon.
friend the Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Sam Hughes) if he has any report to make, or any information to give the House, in regard to the alleged disturbances at Edmonton.

I have no information as to any disturbances at Edmonton. I have heard that threats were made at Edmonton, but I have no report of any [DOT]disturbances whatever. Edmonton is a peaceful and law-abiding city.

If I might take the opportunity of placing before the House the facts in regard to the case, it may clear up some misunderstanding, and I think it would be to th$ general advantage. As there were reports current that there had been a disturbance in that city, it would be just as well for the House to be aware of how that occurred and what the nature of it was. I will take the opportunity of quoting from the Edmonton Bulletin of Saturday, February 12:
Citizens walking down town last night found the unusual spectacle of pickets of soldiers with riilas and bayonets, stationed at the corners where Namayo, Fraser, Queen's,
McDougall and Howard avenues open on to Jasper, to protect property from violence at the hands of a crowd of their comrades.
Two buildings are understood to have been the objectives of the crowd, the Macdonald hotel and the Bulletin office-the hotel because of a report that alien enemies are employed there, and the Bulletin office because some misguided parties had circulated a false report that the paper had referred to the 51st, 63rd and 66th Battalions as "dogs."
The paragraph which was distorted into a cause of offence on the part of the Bulletin appeared in the editorial columns on Wednesday evening and Thursday morning, and was as follows:	.
"The dog is a very useful and estimable animal in his own place. And his place is a large one. But the street of a city is not part ot that place. Child life in this community would be safer and parental life freed from a good deal of worry if the hides of about three battalions of good-for-nothing mongrels were nailed to the fence."
The plain meaning of the paragraph is clear to any one who does not read for the purpose of finding some hidden significance in it, and nothing of this kind, of course, was meant, and when it became known yesterday that some parties had seized upon it as a pretext to stir up antagonism among the soldiers, a protest against the gross misinterpretation was published in the evening edition. ... To Lieut.-Colonel McKinery, commanding officer of the 66th; Lieut.-Colonel Harwood, commanding officer of the 51st; Lieut.-Colonel George McLeod, commanding officer of the 63rd; and Chief of Police Hill is due the fact that the evening's proceedings did not end more disastrously. Chief Hill, upon learning of the trouble that was brewing, at once telephoned the three commanding officers and apprised them of the situation, informing them at the same time that his men would be powerless without military assistance.
Lieut.-Colonel McKinery, of the 66th, immediately jumped into his auto, leaving Major Durrand in charge of the men at the grounds. The colonel upon reaching the danger zone put officers in charge of all the soldiers on leave, with instructions to prevent disturbance. At the same time the men at barracks, under Major Durrand, were marched into the city, and upon arriving at Jasper and Fraser, cleared the street of all soldiers not on duty, at the same time ordering civilians to disperse.	/
The other battalions responded with promptitude, pickets being sent from, each, and stationed at McDougall and Jasper, Howard and Jasper, Queen's and Jasper, and Fraser and jasper-the four points of vantage. Their arrival was not a moment too soon, a crowd of khakied men already having assumed a threatening attitude. They formed, of course, but a small proportion of the total number of soldiers in the city, but their number was sufficiently large to provide considerable excitement for the time being. The pickets remained on duty for some hours after the occurrence, and with aid of a squad of city police, both on foot and mounted, under Inspector Shute, barred the progress of all soldiers along Jasper, from McDougall to Fraser.
Lieut.-Colonel G. B. McLeod, shortly after eight o'clock, arranged for the manager of the Bulletin to address the soldiers who were con-

gregated at Queen's avenue. The manager, in addressing the men, explained that the article to which exception was taken had no reference to the soldiers, which explanation was perfectly satisfactory. The soldiers then dispersed with cheers for the colonel. Colonel McLeod .also addressed the men earlier in the evening explaining that the article was not intended to refer to them.
A number of arrests were made while the excitement was at its height, the persons in question being taken to the city police station.
Part of my reason for bringing this matter to the attention of the minister and the House is to let the facts be known as they really were; and, further, to draw attention to the fact that the instigation of trouble came from outside the military, and not inside. We have some strenuous politics in the city of Edmonton at times, and I do not think there is any doubt that the misinterpretation placed upon the article in question was the deliberate act of some active and measurably clever politicians. I do not wish my hon. friends opposite to think I am associating them with these politicians at all;
I am merely pointing out that in my opinion the trouble arose out of a deliberate attempt on the part of a certain set of men in the city of Edmonton, who are not soldiers, to turn to their own advantage the excitement that grew out of the occurrences in Calgary. At a time such as this, when the country is subject to excitement, there is always an, opportunity for evilly-disposed persons who are not soldiers to arouse antagonism for the purpose of achieving some advantage or revenge for themselves. I think that that is a feature of the case which is absolutely proved by the occurrences in Edmonton, and one which may be found * to be connected with occurrences of perhaps a more serious kind in other places.

speakeroldname: Sir SAM HUGHES (Minister of Militia and Defence):
speechtext:
I had not the detailed information which the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) has given to the House, but I knew that this was nothing more than one of those little scares that occur from time to time in different parts of the country, the public piind being more or less excited. The policy for all wise men such as my hon. friend and others of us to pursue is to keep our heads level.
If he will permit me to say so, I do not know that I would have gone quite as far as my hon. friend in attributing this scare to certain persons, whether in or out of the militia. Any one knowing my hon. friend to be the proprietor and .moving spirit and genius behind the Edmonton

Bulletin, would realize that a great family journal like that could not by any possibility be induced to say anything offensive to the boys out to do their duty for King and country; especially when it is known, not only in that locality but elsewhere, that nearly all the sons and relatives of the hon. member for Edmonton are out doing their duty under the colours to-day.

I should just like to draw the attention of the House to the promptitude and energy with which the officers of these battalions handled the situation. Their action certainly left nothing to be desired.
On the Orders of the Day:

I should like to read a
short paragraph from the Ottawa Free Press of last night:
Pay of Soldiers in Civil Service.
In reply to Mr. J. G. Turriff, who asserted that the Government should put an end to the practice of paying civil servants who are on active service their salaries, Hon. Dr. Roche, Minister of the Interior, in the House of Commons, yesterday afternoon stated that the Government felt it would be a breach of faith if it cancelled the pay of men who enlisted early in the war on the understanding- that their salaries were to be paid.
I did not make any such remarks at all. What I said was this, as will be seen by Hansard:
Mr. Turriff: On what grounds does the Government justify paying a man who enlists on the last day of October both his civil and military pay, and a man who enlists on the 1st of November only his military pay, and the difference between that and his civil pay? If that practice is followed there will be no harmony in the departments of the Government nor in the trenches. I am not speaking particularly against either system, although I think the latter system is the best; but I say that all the men should he treated alike; put them all under one system or under the other. I do not think the present system is fair.
I just wished to correct the impression given by the Free Press last night. I did not request in any shape or form that civil servants who volunteer should not be paid their'civil salaries, but suggested that they should all be put on the same basis.

speakeroldname: Hon. ROBERT ROGERS (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
I received this morning
the report of the architects who have been making an examination of the Parliament

Buildings and, with the consent of the House, I will read it, as it is very short:
The Honourable Robert Rogers,
Minister of Public Works,
Ottawa.
Re Parliament Buildings.
Dear Sir,-We have made a careful examination of the main building that was recently damaged by fire, and beg to report as follows:
The major portion of the buildings at present Teft. standing, more particularly as regards the internal and external walls, have suffered no material damage.
The west wing, which was recently built on modern fireproof methods, is uninjured by fire and but slightly damaged by water.
From this point-viz., the west wing-travelling south to the southwest tower, thence east along the south front to the Southeast tower, thence north to the northeast tower, thence west to the east wall, thence north to the north tower -all these walls which comprise the perimeter of the building are practically intact and uninjured ; it will be only necessary to make repairs to a number of windows on the south front, where the flames have injured the Ohio sandstone trimmings.
Starting at the same point before mentioned -viz., the west wing-and travelling in the same direction : all rooms fronting on these elevations^ have been more or less swept by fire and burned out; the brick masonry in the internal longitudinal and cross walls, also the maftonry in the external walls inclosing these rooms has suffered little damage-the stability of these \Valls has not been impaired.
The character of this masonry, both in material and workmanship, is first class. The external walls are faced with Nepean random rock-faced quarries, with Ohio stone trimmings to window openings ; the walls are backed with rubble, and faced on the inside with brick carefully built and properly bonded into the rubble masonry. It is this facing of brick that has preserved the limestone rubble against damage by fire.
The floors throughout the building are constructed with 7-inch iron I-beam joists spaced eighteen inches on centres, filled in solid with lime mortar concrete, the soffits of the beams exposed.
That the walls have suffered so little damage from the fire, is due to the nature of this construction, which might be termed " semi-fireproof." The floors have not burned through; they have remained in position, and very materially stiffened the building and retarded the fire. But it will be necessary to take out the floors, remove the iron beams and replace with steel beams and fireproof material.
The walls of the main tower are backed up solid with limestone rubble, exposed on the internal face. The fire has done considerable damage to this limestone backing and to the Ohio sandstone around the window openings. It will be necessary to tajte down the spandrel walls between the four corner piers to the level of the sill of the large windows and rebuild.
The area in the heart of the building formerly occupied by the Commons Chamber and the Senate Chamber, from the north wall of the main corridor, " with the exception of the basement and foundation walls," is a total loss.
The building as it stands to-day represents an asset in labour and material in position, of
fully $2,000,000, that can be re-used. The external walls require but few repairs, and when these are made all evidence of fire will be obliterated.
If more accommodation is required in the Commons Chamber and the Senate Chamber, these rooms could be placed on the east and west sides Of the main building carried out in the same style of architecture, and the space * they formerly occupied could be utilized in providing increased office accommodation and stack room for the library.
The Library building is a most dangerous ' fire hazard. The floor, shelving, and roof should be replaced with fireproof material.
Respectfully submitted,
(Sgd.) John A. Pearson. (Sgd.) J. O. Marchand.
Ottawa, February 17, 1916.
On the Orders of the Day:

May I ask the
Minister of Militia whether there is any truth in the rumour which has been circulated to the effect that our Canadian troops have been in an engagement along the line near Ypres, and if so, what information he has on the subject?

We have no official information other than that an attack was made by the enemy on the British and Canadian lines from a point southeast of Ypres for a number of miles. The bombardment was very heavy, lasting for two days and part of the third day. Our troops do not seem to have suffered nearly as much as might have been expected. The first day five or six were killed, and the next day only one; there were fifteen or sixteen wounded. The Germans, following the bombardment, got into our trenches at many points, and my information is that those Germans are still there, but dead.
It is reported that the Germans still hold some of our trenches.
I have no information to that effect. Not a solitary foot of our trenches is in the hands of the enemy,
Consideration of the proposed motion of Sir Thomas White (Minister of Finance) for Committee of Ways and Means, resumed from Tuesday, February 15.

Mr,
Speaker, never perhaps in the history of Canada was a Budget speech looked forward to with such interest as that which the Minister of Finance delivered in this House on Tuesday last. Our financial posi-

tion presently and prospectively is one of gravity and naturally it demands a most serious and thoughtful attention on the part of the Government and of the people. It also intimately involves the immediate and prospective welfare of our people and our country. My remarks shall be of a general rather than of a detailed character, although I hope to deal with some matters of detail for the purpose of amplifying and reenforcing certain general propositions.
The Budget speech of the Minister of Finance was characterized by lucidity and brevity, upon which I heartily congratulate him, although I fear I cannot hope to imitate him.
At the beginning I wish to say a few words in respect to our balance of trade, which has been a favourable one this year, not because it needs be an indication of unusually healthy trade conditions, but for its value in the settlement of international balances and in the stabilization of the exchange rates, which we have learned are so vital to our trade. For these reasons, the relations of imports to exports during the present year is, in the circumstances, gratifying. It must be remembered, however, that imports and exports are not solely determined by customs returns. For the nine months ending December 31 last, our imports, free and dutiable^ amounted to $348,746,000, while our exports amounted to $511,334,000, showing thus far a favourable trade balance of over $160,000,000, and at the end of the fiscal year it will be over $200,000,000. When we borrow money we export securities, which is just the same as'the export of wheat except that payment in the former case is deferred. The annual interest is an import exactly in the same sense that cotton is an import. The total of annual interest payable on Canadian securities to Great Britain amounts probably to $150,000,000, and to the United States $40,000,000, both of which must be calculated as annual imports. In addition to this we pay to foreign countries for services of one kind or another, such as brokerage, shipping and insurance, a very considerable sum. Keeping these matters in view, we must not conclude that we have become a creditor nation by reason merely of an excess in exports over imports in merchandise during the present fiscal year.
Neither should we be led astray in our calculations of the future by the trade figures and trade balances of this year. We had an abundant harvest. The trade activities of the United States were reflected

here, and the export of war supplies reached unexpected levels, all of which largely accounted for the volume of our exports and imports. It is generally conceded that our exportable crops for the present calendar year cannot equal in proportions those . of last year and consequently our exports and imports will be affected, for we can only pay for imports with our exports or by borrowing abroad. Neither should we rely too much upon the continuance of war supply exports. The Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) was quite frank last week in expressing his opinion about the duration of the war, and many are the evidences that it may continue even longer than he indicated. His statement, which I assume was not merely a personal opinion, was one of the most impressive and .pregnant ever made to the people of Canada. It is well known that the strength of Germany's position at present is in the fact that she is not an importer, and consequently does not export gold except in negligible quantities. This will enable her to continue the war much longer than if she were an importing country with international balances to settle. The economic strain upon Great Britain is tremendous, and nothing produces greater problems than the exchange question, because in the main she must pay for her abnormal imports by exports of goods or securities and not with gold, and she is constantly devising means of limiting imports. For instance last year very high import duties were placed upon certain commodities which might be classified as luxuries, or, at least, were not actual necessities. These tariff rates were not imposed for purposes of protection or revenue, but to diminish imports in order to stabilize, if possible, the sterling exchange, or in other words to reduce the spread between imports and exports. A proclamation was issued in Great Britain on Tuesday last prohibiting the import, after March 1, next, of paper, paper pulp, periodicals, tobacco, furniture, wood and stone. Only last week Sir Alfred Booth, chairman of the board of directors of the Cunard Steamship Company, publicly urged individual thrift by taxation. That is, he urged such an increase in taxation as would minimise consumption and importation. What does this indicate? It is a warning that Britain, so far as possible, must be self-contained and that her war and other necessities must be manufactured within herself, so far as possible. In the event of a protracted struggle this will, in some degree happen, and war orders in

"Canada will diminish as will our exports, unless possibly we are able to accept British securities in payment of the same, which is unlikely. If this adversely affects the United States we shall also share in the adversity. What then will be our position?
I need not say to honourable gentlemen it will be serious. Manufacturing for other allied nations is always susceptible to shocks, through the condition of the exchange rates which are liable at any moment to severe changes. In that event we cannot manufacture profitably unless we are able to accept payment in foreign securities and it is doubtful that this will be possible. I refer to these matters at this length to point out to the House that the present trade conditions are liable to rapid changes, and soon we may be confronted with a changed situation. I refer to it also in order to impress upon the Government and the country the necessity of rigid- national economy and the abandonment of many practices in our financial affairs in which we now engage, but to which I * shall later refer.
In respect to the domestic loan of $100,000,000, I have just a few words to say, all of which I very modestly submit. 1 think undoubtedly the Minister of Finance was justified in making the loan a domestic one, and all Canadians were proud of its success. Doubtless by this time a substantial portion of it has been purchased for United States account, and we have thus been relieved in part. The time was a favourable one for a domestic loan, on account of our magnificent crop and favourable trade balance, and another opportunity for a domestic loan equally as favourable may not soon appear again. The investing capacity of the Canadian public is limited; consequently there is a limit to Government domestic loans. Unless Canadians are impressed with the necessity of economy, and make investments in domestic loans from savings, our national financial position is not much improved by subscriptions to domestic loans. If subscriptions for domestic war loans come largely from our banks and financial institutions, directly or indirectly, no bene-" fit accrues to the country; although, oi course, the immediate credit required is obtained by the Government. Now, wealth cannot be created in this manner. All funds disbursed on account of war loan subscriptions by banks soon return to the banks, who have the securities as well; so that there is a tendency to inflation. Again, banking capital and reserves in
Canada play too big a part in our business affairs to be absorbed appreciably in war loans. The banks, in any event, can retain only such portion of the war loan as they actually desire, an.(l must dispose of the balance; so it is better in the first instance to have the loan placed .in the investor's hands. Too great a proportion of this loan was subscribed for by our banks, which seem' to have subscribed upon some uniform basis, giving their subscriptions the appearance of having been involuntary. True, the loan was a success from the Government standpoint, but not from the national standpoint. It was a success only because a large number of people accustomed to investing subscribed from business and patriotic motives, and because large financial institutions subscribed heavily. It was not a success in the more important sense, however, that subscriptions came from the small investor .and represented savings and permanent investment. The sale of high interest-bearing government securities afforded a great opportunity to cultivate the spirit of investment and economy among the people of small holdings; this class were not properly considered in connection with the loan. This was the first opportunity that ever came to Canada to encourage national thrift and investment among persons of small means; a splendid opportunity for an educative campaign was neglected. The prospectus issued was stereotyped and more intended for underwriters than investors.
I do not think the Minister of Finance made the proper preparations
4 p.m. for this loan. A campaign widespread and enthusiastic by various mediums should have been undertaken. The services of hundreds of Canadians might, on request, have been enlisted to carry on a campaign for the Government in connection with this loan. Canadians are not exemplars, perhaps, in private economics; but I think they are ready, for economic and patriotic reasons, to forego much in order to ensure the success of Canadian war loans. I think they would be quite responsive to a campaign for this purpose, and the economic effect upon the nation would be visible for years. It would be most disastrous, I say, to have a series of large loans mainly subscribed by banks and financial institutions directly or indirectly. This loan, while widely subscribed, was not in the real sense a popular loan, and no proper effect was made to make it such. We must borrow on our own market for other purposes. In 1915 Canada bor-

rowed on issued securities $340,000,000, of which $150,000,000 was supplied by Canada herself. Therefore, I say that in future some organized effort should be made well in advance to make subscriptions for government loans bearing high interest rates more popular and general, and, so far as possible, to haye them come from savings. There are other features of this loan that might profitably be discussed, but returns asked for in respect to it have not yet been brought down, and later in the session we shall probably return to a discussion of its terms.
I wish now to refer to the financial statement just presented by the Minister of Finance in respect to the present fiscal year. The minister's statement that there was a surplus of $45,000,000 of revenue over ordinary expenditure was presented, quite adroitly though not too frankly, and received by hon. gentlemen opposite as a great financial feat. But it must be noted that, including all domestic or civil expenditure, the surplus will be, roughly, but $5,000,000; and that, inclusive of war expenditures, the deficit will be about $125,000,000. It is further to be noted that this surplus was procured by taxation, not by economies in expenditures. The surplus of $45,000,000 is a delusion and a fallacy, and hon. gentlemen know it. They did not reduce ordinary expenditure; the revenue came from the people, not from the Government. The Minister of Finance did not, I think, take sufficient pains to make it clear that capital expenditures were made from borrowed capital, which would wipe out the surplus over ordinary expenditures. Having in mind the method of accounting employed by the Minister of Finance, let me ask this question: if a surplus of $45,000,000 over ordinary expenditure was gratifying, would not a surplus of $75,(300,000 or $80,000,000 have been even more gratifying? That would mean bringing the ordinary expenditure down to about $75,000,000, which it was in 1907-08. Is it not reasonable to say that this might easily have been done? There was an opportunity to produce such a surplus, because the gross^ revenue was the highest in the history of the country; but, unfortunately, our total ordinary expenditures practically reached the highest mark. The war has destroyed a great many systems and theories, and one, I think, which ought to become a thing'of the past is our system of national bookkeeping. The Minister of Finance presented us with three different sets of accounts, consolidated fund, capital expenditures, and war ex-
penditures; showing them all separately, one at a time. If they had been shown together, they would disclose an excess of total expenditure over revenue of $125,000,000. I think the people of Canada desire to know this, and not what happens to be the difference between revenue and what we call ordinary expenditure. They want the cards showing our financial position placed on the table face up, which I do not think was done by the Minister of Finance.
I submit that the proper system is to treat war expenditure in the budget statement as a current one, and on that basis we find that for the fiscal year ending March 31, next, we have a tremendous gap between income and outgo. We know such expenditures will be added largely to the debt, but, we had better look at it in the way I have indicated. There will then be no humbugging of the tax payer, and no political pyrotechnics in this House, or out, side.
The Minister of Finance has informed the House that he is gratified with the result of the taxation measures of last year. In this I partially, but not wholly, agree with him, particularly with reference to his additional tariff taxation. It is regrettable that we have such scanty information in respect to the effect of the tariff taxation imposed last year. We were informed by the Minister of Finance in his last Budget speech, that the Trade and Navigation returns would contain the result of the war tariff rates, but no such information is supplied, and consequently it is difficult to deal with the matter intelligently, although a return submitted to the House furnished some general information.
Let me deal with the tariff taxation first. Undoubtedly the war tariff tax produced considerable revenue, nearly twenty millions of dollars up to January last; and, particularly, I would say the 74 per cent tariff on articles formerly free produced considerable revenue, probably three-fourths of the total. The effect of the surtax of 74 per cent upon the general tariff rates did not prove, I believe, a gain to revenue, and it undoubtedly restricted trade. Again, on account of the high prices ruling in respect to almost all commodities, the increased tariff rates added much to the cost and value of importations. There were very considerable importations into Canada of raw materials entering into the manufac- ' ture of war materials, and the additional tariff increased materially the prices. It

added to [DOT] the cost of war supplies which we purchased ourselves, and to the amount which we must also pay to the British Government as our proportion. So while we received some additional revenue by reason of the war tariff taxation, yet it was paid out again, and more perhaps, in addition to co_st of war supplies, and consequently we are little better off. In this respect the statistics do not disclose the full facts, and it is difficult to estimate the net results of much of the tariff taxation imposed last year. Again there were drawbacks, upon exported war materials which will probably amount to six or seven million dollars for the year, so therefore I say that at, least the extra 74 per cent added to the general tariff yielded practically no revenue, and was an impediment to trade. We took the position, last year, that the indiscriminate application of 74 per cent to free and dutiable goods was inadvisable and indefensible, and we still say so. It was not based on any sound business principle. It imposed unnecessary burdens upon trade, and was not a success in producing revenue in proportion to the burdens imposed; in fact, but for the tariff on free goods, little increase of revenue, if any, would have resulted. A considered and discriminating tariff measure for revenue' purposes was possible, but this was not of that character. In framing that extra tariff taxation, the Minister of Finance took the easy course, not the businesslike one.
Last year when the minister imposed the new tariff rates, he expressed, amidst the acclaim of his friends, the belief that it would be efficacious in stimulating Canadian industry and agriculture, and in relieving unemployment. This sounded then to me more like the idle prophecy of the politician than the remarks of a capable financial administrator. We have not heard of that prophecy this year. After the passing of almost a year, I am sure honourable gentlemen opposite will agree with me that this prediction was idle, as was expected, and that any stimulation that came to Canadian industry, or any relief that came to unemployment, was not the result of the tariff taxation measure of last year, but one of the incidents of a worldwide calamity; and further, that any stimulation that came to Canadian agriculture was due to the efforts of men and the blessings of God, and not to the tariff of the Minister of Finance.

Now, what was the true financial policy for the Government during the past two years in view of the war and the commercial conditions immediately preceding the war? What is the true policy for the future? I say it was and is rigid economy in civil expenditures, the elimination of unnecessary capital expenditures, the elimination of wastes in war expenditures, and the utmost of proper and wise taxation to lessen the addition to the public debt. This policy has not been followed, and there is nothing to indicate an intention to follow it during the next fiscal year; but I shall refer to this later.
This is, perhaps, the most convenient place for me to make reference to the Estimates for the coming fiscal year, which are open to grave censure, and are outiof harmony with public opinion. The Estimates of ordinary expenditure for the coming year amount to $158,958,000, the largest in our history. There is an increase of $16,000,000 for interest upon the public debt, and there are miscellaneous increases and reductions in the various services, leaving a net estimated increase for ordinary expenditure of over $8,250,000 more than for the present year. The Estimates are objectionable in that they do not show sufficient reduction. The Government reply that much of the money voted is but revotes, and will not be spent. My reply is that votes representing expenditures which are not to be made have no place in the Budget system. Further, the Minister of Finance estimates ordinary expenditures bf $135,000,000 for next year, which, I say,
[Mr. A. K. Maclean.!
are excessive. Further, the Government have no right to ask Parliament to vote money which they say they will not likely expend.
No other spending body is permitted to' do /this. If the budget system has- any virtues, estimates should only contain/ actual necessities and should represent actual intentions. It encourages departmental extravagances and wasteful expenditure, it is an encouragement to the evils of patronage, it prolongs the hope for unprofitable expenditures in the minds of many people and localities, and postpones-the day when we should and must revise our policy upon public expenditures.
Many leaders of public opinion are requesting economies on the part of the people. Should not the Government show capacity for leadership? Would it not very materially help our credit to show substan-tiai surpluses over all civil expenditures?' When the Minister of Finance made his-loan of $45,000,000 in New York last July,. I understand that Mir. J..P. Morgan & Company sent their representatives here to investigate the revenues and expenditures of the country. ' Street rumour has it that they were astounded at the vast sums of' money expended in this country for unproductive purposes. The Minister of Finance will some day soon be seeking another substantial loan in the United States. Does he think our estimates for next year would strengtheif our credit in the judgment of possible lenders? Would the estimates of expenditure on ordinary account tend to elevate the opinion of foreign lenders in our spending wisdom particularly after a perusal of the items referable to public buildings and harbours and rivers? Should not national credit, /always based, on revenue, .be properly cared for and nursed? Would the defence avail that many items would not be expended? I submit that the estimates in the present form are indefensible, and Parliament should not be asked to vote them. Why should we be asked to vote supply in the sum of $158,000,000 for next year greater by $8,000,000 than last year when admittedly it is not needed?' Only ten years ago our ordinary expenditure was $67,000,000. Why not revert to something like that basis-of expenditure again for a few years? If we did so our estimates could be below or around $100,000,000 instead of $158,000,000, after making ample provision, for an increase of $28,000,000 in the interest, and pension accounts since that date.

For another reason I should like to see business and conscience introduced into our Estimate of expenditure. It is too true that in Canada large sums of money are spent by government which are not only unproductive in the material sense, but which in the moral sense are demoralising. It is the genesis of patronage and electoral corruption. Cobden once truly remarked that public economy is public virtue. I am not now engaging in the unprofitable task of accusing the present Administration of being more guilty than others. But when and where is it going to end? Is this not the time in our history when reforms should appear, and should not we who are here to-day as the people's representatives avail ourselves of this opportunity to do real service to the state, now and hereafter? I think all reflecting men have thought more of this during the past few months than ever before in their lives. Surely the fact that many of our citizens are sacrificing their lives for the nation and for principle should prompt us to adopt higher principles in public expenditures, to deal more justly with the taxes of the public, and save democracy from the corrupting influences flowing from improperly expended public moneys. Should not members of Parliament be leaders in the movement? Honourable gentlemen opposite will retort that it is easier for one in opposition to the Government to speak in this manner. I think that is quite true. 1 want to be frank. I must say that I never before realized the force of political patronage as I have since the beginning of the war. I do not say patronage enters into everything, nor do I mean to say that many men supporting the Government are not fighting against it. I mean only to say that as a fact it exists, and in disgusting proportions. I have seen the evil of political patronage in recent months in little and in large transactions. I know of some ministers who have resisted the pressure made upon them by their friends for improper expenditures, and I know of other ministers who have succumbed to these attacks. And I ask again, when is it going to end? Why not now? Is not this the time to commence? I think so, and believe that a large section of the public would rally to the support of any such reform. The revotes in this year's Estimates, however, is but a token of the continuance of past practices, and for this reason I say the Government is open to grave censure. Is there a better way, after all, to stay improper expenditure than to stop the sources of its origin? The Estimates of the Canadian Parliament is the book to read and to revise if we want to bring about reform in public expenditure, the reduction of patronage evils, and generally political and commercial corruption; for political life is not alone in need of regeneration in Canada. I need not, I hope, apologize for this diversion, for, after all, it strictly pertains to the budget, and the welfare of the country.
I must return to a discussion of the expenditure, and I should like to illustrate the position I have already taken in respect to expenditures by reference to the administration of a few of the public services.
I shall first refer to the administration of the Post Office Department, which in the past two or three years presents a most discreditable record. The decline in Sound administration in this department commenced when Hon Louis Phillippe Pelletier became Postmaster General. He took general conduct of the department away from his officials, and handed it over to patronage brokers all the way from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and his ears were always ready to heed their requests. The Post Office Department, for many years, had an honourable administrative career, but this has been deliberately destroyed, and an era of chaos established. The present Postmaster General apparently entertains his official duties but lightly, and has made no effort to restore sound business principles to the administration of his department. Since 1867 the revenue from the post office has yearly grown, and the expenditures, of course, as well. Since 1902 down to last year the department has always had a yearly surplus of about $700,000. In 1914 the surplus had fallen to the ominous .sum of $134,000. For the fiscal year ending March 31, 1915, we were made acquainted with a deficit of $2,914,541.90, being almost four hundred per cent greater than the greatest deficit known to the department since 1867.
It is difficult to estimate the probable deficit of the department for the fiscal year ending March 31 next, because it is difficult to allocate the total revenues coming to the Post Office Department from its own earnings and that of the war stamp tax^s. I estimate that a strict accounting would show a deficit for the present fiscal year of $5,000,000, and perhaps more. It will be difficult, perhaps, to estimate with accuracy the exact postal revenue for this

year. From the postage on letters thirty-three and a third per cent belongs to war revenue; one-half of the revenue from postal cards and drop letters does not belong to the Post Office Department. The revenue coming from the use of stamps upon cheques, notes, money orders, postal notes, patent medicine packages, perfumery, and wines-and the amount in the hands of the Post Office Department is large-was dedicated to war and not to departmental incompetency and inefficiency.
In the fiscal year 1915 the expenditures were nearly three million dollars greater than revenue, without apparently any visible reason. The revenue had not fallen below that of 1914. There had been no notable increase in the services of the department; in fact, there were many declines. The increase in the expenditure was not due to the war, because the special services of the department in this respect were liquidated by capital account. It was due to the effect that the department has been sold to party patronage. Since honourable gentlemen have been placed on the treasury benches, mail contracts have been violated and transferred at higher cost to political friends; the system of tender and contract has been largely abandoned, and the administration of the department has become a public scandal, and it is a fitting subject for investigation by the Public Accounts Committee or by a Royal Commission. I quite understand why the Minister of Finance asked the public to lick an extra stamp during the past ten months, and I said so last year. He did not trust the Post Office Department and thought he could earmark war-tax stamps. But he failed. The Post Office Department kept the revenue, and it thought it was rich and grew extravagant and wasted the revenue from the stamp taxes of the Minister of Finance. That department will owe the Receiver General at least $5,000,000 at the end of March, but it will not be paid over.
Just a passing review of the administration of the Dominion lands, which branch of the Interior Department has been the victim of reckless partisan administration. In the last fiscal year we had a deficit of over $800,000 in this branch of the public service, and it was only the second deficit since 1885. Now, this condition of affairs was not due to unusual burdens thrust upon the Department of the Interior. The homestead entries made in 1915 were but 24,088 as against 33,699 in 1913, the acreage homesteaded in 1913 being 5,391,840 acres, as against 3,854,00 acres in 1915. This depart-

ment of the public service has a declining business and it should have a declining expenditure. Still, we are asked to vote the large sum of $3,304,000 for next year. I submit that vote should be less by more than one million dollars. Not to reduce it is but paying tribute to departmental waste, and putting temptation in the way of a department already possessing a highly overloaded service. I protest against such a system of budget making.

The Government preach public economy, but do not practise jt; they preach private economy, but do not encourage it. The country looks to the Government for

We owe it to the cause for which we fight, and we owe it to posterity, that we pay something on this account. 5 p.m. we have not sought to reduce.

This brings me to a brief consideration 6f the taxation proposals that the Minister of Finance submitted on Tuesday last. A proper discussion of these proposals involves a considerable amount of investigation and thought, which I at least have not been able to give to the matter since the proposals were brought down. I propose, therefore, referring to them only in a general way, anticipating that in Committee of Ways and Means we shall have an opportunity of discussing them in detail.
In respect to the proposed duties upon apples and certain kinds of oil, I have the general observation to make that if this proposed taxation is made for political effect, or for purposes of protection rather than of revenue, it is objectionable. The Minister of Finance said the other day that it was absolutely necessary for the apple industry of Canada that the additional duty should be imposed. In my judgment, in no province of Canada outside of British Columbia are the apple growers interested in this increased duty. To say that the proposed increase would be of any value to the apple producers of the province of Nova Scotia, for instance, is to state a manifest absurdity. I do not believe that the imposition of this duty will be of any -advantage to the apple industry of British Columbia. It will limit consumption; it will not provide a market for the surplus production-and this, I believe, is the great difficulty which the apple industry encountered during the past season. This additional tax upon apples must be borne by the three prairie provinces; it must have been designed to that' end. It must have been intended to limit the consumers of the three prairie provinces to one source of apple supply, namely, the province of British Columbia. Apparently the people of the prairie provinces receive very few, if any, favours or concessions from this Government in respect of tariffs or taxation. We expect the people of these provinces to increase production in order that we may pay for our imports, but we do little or nothing to encourage them to this patriotic end. Further, apples are a staple food; it is to be remembered that the staple foodstuffs of the country are to-day exceedingly high. I am not going to discuss the matter of tariffs, but I do submit that, having regard to the trade and revenue of this country, a limited readjustment of several items in the tariff, particularly 574
those affecting staple foodstuffs, might have been expected this year. We- are-apt to think that mo-st of the people? of this country are extremely prosperous. I want to point out that, owing to war prices, the struggle for existence on the part of many people in this country is extremely serious. In the case of such a prime necessity as potatoes, for instance, the price to-day is almost prohibitive, and in view of the limited production of potatoes last year I was very much disappointed that the Minister of Finance did not, last fall, invoke the power given to him and by Order in Council temporarily at least remove the duty upon this staple foodstuff.
I have not made any special inquiry as to the effect of the extra duty on oil. Ii it was- intended for protective and not for revenue purposes, I say it is objectionable. I am informed that it will apply chiefly to fuel used by locomotives and steamships. It appears to me that this is an inopportune time to add any additional taxation to transportation bodies. There is a rumor on the street that this tax was a concession to the coal interests of British Columbia. I trust that that is not the reason for it. We were given no reason by the Minister of Finance, and I think we are entitled to it; but I assume we will get it in committee. I think it would be quite interesting to know the reason for the imposition of a tax upon oil which is largely consumed by transportation organizations that are not in too favourable a position at present, and also by some farmers for power purposes.
I wish to refer briefly and generally to the taxation of profits on manufacturing and trading concerns. I admit that any system of taxation is unpopular and open to criticism from some source or another. In respect to the proposals of the Government to impose a tax upon business profits, I do not wish to be understood as saying that they are absolutely without merit. In my judgment, howeve,, they are in many respects fundamentally wrong; they contain many inequalities which will work great injustice, and, in my judgment, they will not be so effective in producing revenue as the Minister of Finance estimates. The great obejction to the taxation of profits, as proposed, is that it is a tax upon business, and not upon accumulated wealth, or upon the income proceeding from accumulated wealth. I say that the proposal to tax profits on business is, at the best, but a temporary expedient
900 '

[ think I can safely say that for .some years to .come, after the war ends, this country will have to resort for revenue to sources other than tariff, and we might as well, now as later, settle down to elaborate some comprehensive system of taxation which will afford this country the additional revenue required for its national needs, over iand a'bove that which we might naturally expect to accrue from tariff taxation.
In respect to the retroactive feature of the tax proposals, I would like to express a view, even if it be but a personal view, against the principle. I submit Mr. Speaker, that never, except in grave circumstances, and under grave necessities, should taxation proposals be retroactive. If, owing to lax administration by this Government, Canada or Great Britain was permitted to pay improper and unjust profits upon war supplies, it might be proper that we should seek restitution by the medium of taxation measures. That, however, is no defence of the principle of retroactive taxation, it is only a recognition of culpability on the part of the Government in the performance of their administrative duties. The Minister of Finance attempted the same thing in connection with his excise duties in 1914, and my recollection is that he absolutely failed to recover any substantial sum of revenue for removals from warehouses just prior to the imposition of the additional duties.
There is, further, this to say, Mr. Speaker, in connection with this feature of the proposed taxation, that it will not, after all, produce very much revenue. You will find that the large transportation companies, and the large industrial organizations, for many months, probably for twelve months at least, after war was declared, were not earning profits, or if they were, they were very small profits. Perhaps they were borrowing capital in order to carry on their businesses. The only business eonoernis conducted with any possible hope of profit were the smaller business concerns of the country, and the retroactive feature of the tax proposals will, I predict, fall upon the smaller concerns; and in such cases the profits were long ago disbursed. Whatever be our necessities for revenue, I submit that it will be a grave injustice to compel payment of disbursed profits by these small organizations to the treasury under such conditions.
Further, I submit that these taxation proposals will disclose many inequalities which will operate unjustly, and will not
[Mr A. K, Maclean.]
properly distribute the burden of taxation as intended by the principle of the Bill. The capitalization of many of our large industrial and trading concerns to-day does not represent actual investment in capital or of earnings, but these concerns will be entitled to a profit o'f 7 per cent upon all watered stock before they become liable to the provisions of the tax bill. In many cases the larger corporations are paying no dividend upon their common stock. This proposal is in effect a premium upon improper methods of industrial finance and industrial inefficiency. It is not calculated to encourage fair capitalization methods. To show how it will operate, let us take the railways. It is probably the ease that no railway company in Canada, outside of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, will be called upon to pay one dollar of taxes-I am not speaking of street railways -although it may be possible that by reason of the war the Canadian Northern, or the Grand Trunk may have earned very much more than did the Canadian Pacific railway from traffic directly traceable to the war. In the city of Ottawa there is a corporation, the E. B. Eddy Company, and I am told that they have a capitalization of $300,000 or $400,000. Their assets are enormous and their earning capacity very considerable. In that case the amount of taxation for which this company would be liable over the 7 per cent margin would necessarily be very great. Take the case of a corporation with a capitalization of $15,000,000, of which one-half, $7,500,000, represents the actual capital investment, the balance representing nothing but inflated capital; under the terms of the taxation proposal, $7,500,000 of this capital which did n<5t represent any investment would call for a dividend of over $500,000 upon a 7 per cent basis before anything came to the revenues. You will realise how unjust this wuuld appear to be when you consider how it would work out in the case of the E. B. Eddy Company, Limited.
Further, in this country, you will find many companies, partnerships, and private businesses, carried on where the capital investment may be small-below $50,000. It may happen that you will find one man in a community carrying on a line of business, who will be taxed because he has a capital investment of $50,000. In the same community he may have twelve competitors with a capital investment just slightly less, and they will escape taxation altogether. You may find one class of storekeeper liable

to taxation and many other of the same class will escape. You are bound to find so many inequalities of the character I have described that the proposals are open to very grave objections. We can well imagine the case of a man carrying on an industry with a capital investment of $50,000, the most of which will be in the form of buildings and land, he not requiring very much machinery, and in the same block you may have a man owning $1,000,000 of real estate, which represents a small original investment, the unearned increment being large, and still he is not taxed, whereas the man with the property worth $50,000 is taxed because it happens he is carrying on business of some kind.
War supplies and munitions as sources of revenue were - much discussed by the public long before the Minister of Finance brought down his taxation measure. Personally, I have not been very much impressed with the validity of the popular view justifying such taxation. It was always suggestive to me of the idea that we are deliberately permitting those who manufacture or supply war material to the Canadian and British Governments to take an unjust profit. I have always thought, and I now think, it would be wiser, from the standpoint of the Treasury, instead of depending upon the doubtful method of restitution by ordinary taxation schemes, not to permit these unjust profits to go to the manufacturer of war supplies. There may be very good reasons for allowing a manufacturer of war supplies more than an ordinary profit. We all can conceive of good reasons why he would be entitled to more than seven per cent profit. I say allow them, in the first instance a just profit; do not allow a profit which is unjust and unfair, and then take it back from them by taxation routes. What, is a fair profit should be easy to determine. When a manufacturer proceeds' to fill a specified and guaranteed order he should be able to determine production costs very much more accurately than a person who manufactures'for stock, and who must assume all the risks and responsibilities until that stock has been sold, marketed and paid for. It should be quite easy now to enter into contracts for the supply of war materials at prices which would be fair to the manufacturer and to Canada or the United Kingdom. Therefore, let us pay just prices for our war supplies, and let us not make a readjustment of prices by a system of taxation. In other words, good administration is much more profitable to
the treasury than any taxation -scheme the Minister of Finance can devise. -Another objection which I have to make against these taxation proposals is that they Will militate against foreign and domestic investment in railway and industrial enterprises in Canada. Perhaps I may be unduly alarmed about this, but I fear such a consequence, and if so it is a serious one. Last year, outside of Government and war loans, we borrowed for railway and industrial purposes $60,000,000, and I imagine that practically every cent of it came from the United States. Many industrial companies in Canada will borrow additional capital for many years to come. I fear that this tax upon industrial profits, for a time at least, will prevent the flow of capital from the United States. Is this the time to discourage the investment of capital for industrial purposes? Is it the time,to put a tax upon business profits? Our industrial enterprises in Canada will want further capital from abroad. Conditions are not to be found in Canada as they are in Great Britain, for instance, where most of the industrial institutions are old, have sufficient capital, and where a great majority of them have long established reserves. That is not the case in this country. There is this to be remembered too, that money invested in industrial enterprises naturally and properly looks for a greater return than seven per cent. There is too great a risk in industrial enterprises to satisfy capital with a return, of seven per cent. Business concerns retain out of profits only what they require for the purpose of capital and the proper conduct of their business; the greater portion of the earnings of all industrial companies is disbursed in the form of dividends. Business without the necessary capital is not a desirable thing in this or any other country. If the two premises I have stated are correct, the profits which any business makes are paid out, and could therefore be taxed under any general income tax scheme. Besides, such a scheme would be a more equitable and just manner of taxation, and would not involve the invidious discriminations that the present proposals will likely entail.
There is this further to be said against the proposals of the minister: they do not reach the great bulk of inherited and invested wealth. They do not reach, for instance, the vast aggregation of secured investments in industrial enterprises, or property of one kind or another. I do submit that it is hardly fair that the holders of invested

wealth should escape taxation, as they will under the proposals of the minister. Many other classes are exempted, which appears invidious, though I cannot detain the House now in discussing them.
It might fairly be asked whether the taxation proposals of the Finance Minister might not be modified so as to be mdre just and less discriminatory. I should like to read to the House what the Finance Minister said on Tuesday last in regard to the taxation of industrial companies:
Now, Mr. Speaker, there are in time of war many businesses and industries which for one reason or another are able to maintain profits above the average return to capital in time of
peace.
-that is, in times of war, the Minister of Finance remarks, it is the good fortune of many business concerns to be able to maintain profits above the average of peace times. If it were these profits which the minister sought to tax, he has failed to accomplish that end by the terms of the resolution which he submitted to the House. It is perfectly obvious that there are scores of companies in this country which, during the war, have been making profits much in excess of peace time profits, and under the proposals of the Minister of Finance these profits will not be taxed. It is hard to understand why, in my province, for instance, the Nova Scotia Steel Company should pay a tax upon its profits, and the Dominion Iron and Steel Company probably escape, although it might make very considerable profits also.
I could cite many probable instances of such unequalities. If the minister desired to secure a portion of the war-time profits which were above the average of the profits of peace time, there would be some equity in that, and I could understand it. That is the principle involved in a British Tax Bill introduced last year. There they tax a proportion of the profits made in war time which is above the average of peace time profits; and in order to procure the average peace time profits, they take a period of three years immediately preceding the war. I say it is unjust and discriminatory to tax the profits of a portion of the manufacturing and business concerns, and allow a great many others to escape taxation. The minister could easily prevent that by disregarding capitalization entirely, and taxing war time profits which are in excess of the average of peace time profits; there. is a good deal to be said in favour of that principle.
IMr. A. K. Maclean.]
There might, of course, be a great deal more said upon the taxation measures which the minister has submitted to the House, but they will doubtless be discussed by other hon. gentlemen of the House; and, furthermore, we shall have another opportunity of discussing them, and with greater satisfaction perhaps, in Committee of Ways and Means. It seems to me that, in view of the many weak principles which are obviously contained in the proposals of the Minister of Finance, in view of the many inequalities and discriminations, in view of the fact that hereafter in this country we shall for many years require more revenue than we can possibly secure from Customs and Excise, we might as well begin now and adopt a broad system of taxation based upon income, which would reach aill persons in equitable proportions and without any discriminations. By such a method, we should reach the very business concerns which the minister is attempting to reach by his proposals, but in a much better and more just manner. The minister will probably find that next year he will have to invoke some system of direct income taxation. He has always objected that it was a system of taxation already employed by provinces and municipalities, and was not now open for federal purposes. Theoretically, the income tax is in operation in some of the provinces; but theoretically only. In my own province we have the income tax; but, practically speaking, there is no income taxation. I am informed that the revenue from income taxation in British Columbia is quite substantial, but taxation is taxation no matter under what name it is imposed. I am unable to perceive that there is very much difference between paying a federal tax on income, and a tax in equal amount known by some other name. I do not think the reasons which the minister urged last year, and to which he briefly referred again this year, are sound objections against the immediate imposition of a federal income tax.
In conclusion, let me say that Canada is participating in this great European war with a zeal which I think is quite remarkable. For us, this is not a war of aggression, nor a war of self preservation erffen; it is a war for the preservation of human liberties and civilization; and it is because we are fighting for such high ideals that we are willing to contribute most

generously of our resources. But while we are seeking to accomplish these very commendable ends, we must not recklessly dissipate our resources and revenue in doubtful and dubious expenditure. We should place national expenditure on a sound and businesslike basis, and upon a level and up to a standard which heretofore it has never reached. We 'are engaged in a contest of great magnitude which will undoubtedly entail heavy burdens upon ourselves and posterity. I think that we ought now to bear our just proportion. With the war over and the battle won, our future depends much on our ability to provide the capital that is necessary to proceed with the development of a large and new country, which in all human probability will be receiving but a very limited immigration for many years. Our ability to do that will largely depend on the financial course which we pursue to-day. Now, does the Government's financial attitude of the last few years, particularly in respect to expenditures, indicate a full appreciation of present circumstances and a proper perspective of the future? In all frankness, I think the Government have not realized their responsibilities in that regard, and that, I believe, will be the judgment of the future, if there be any doubt about it to-day.
It has been my purpose during my remarks, which have occupied far more time than I had intended, to impress upon Parliament these two points, namely: the desirability of national economy, the proper conservation of the revenues of the country, so as to limit the taxatioh which must be imposed * upon the people, and at the same time the desirability of placing upon the people that volume of taxation which they can reasonably stand, in order that we may do our duty towards the cause for which we are fighting and towards posterity by paying a reasonable proportion of the war expenditures which are to-day being incurred and which are being added to the national debt of the country.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the moderate and somewhat careful review made by my hon. friend (Mr. A. K. Maclean) of the proposals which were submitted by the Minister of Finance on Tuesday last. In some things that he has stated, I agree with him; as regards others, I would express a mild dissent. There may even be
some points in reference to which I would be inclined to make a rather decided and emphatic protest, but that does not take away from my first remark that I have appreciated and been interested in his line of thought as expressed in his remarks on the Budget.
In the first place, and before going further, I think I may take it upon myself to say that, in so far as I can judge, the spirit with which the Canadian people have met the taxation proposals of last year and of this year is in eminent accord with the spirit in which they have supported enlistment with the colours, and the prosecution of the war. Taxation, whenever it comes, is apt to hit someone harder than another; it is a thing which most poeple would rather not encounter, hut I am convinced that, in so far as the prosecution of this war is concerned, either by the active one hundred thousand, or the two hundred thousand, or the ultimate three or four hundred thousand that go to the front, the seven million five hundred thousand who remain at home are prepared to cheerfully pay what is necessary in order that the men at the front may do their work.	.
My hon. friend took up, first, the balance of trade, and he rather belittled the statement that the balance of trade in this country in the last two years, and notably in the last year, has been so changed that from a large adverse balance of trade, as shown by the imports and exports, we have to-day a large and gratifying favourable balance of trade. It does not depreciate that result in the least to cite the invisible imports and exports, 'and to endeavour to detract from the favourable nature of the present balance of trade by declaring that it does not express the . true state of the exchanges between Canada and outside countries. These invisible imports and exports have been factors in these interchanges during every year that we have existed as a country; they have been increasing factors in these interchanges during the last fifteen or twenty years, and they have been rapidly increasing'factors owing to causes which we all understand. But what we can feel thankful for is that, along with the existence of about equal factors of invisible imports and exports; the situation has so far improved that we have a favourable balance of the imports and exports as shown by the customs returns, and that we have reversed the old situation. Therefore, if there is

any advantage in a favourable balance of trade, that advantge has accrued to Canada during this year.
That "if" is the point.

My hon. friend (Mr. A. K. Maclean) made some remarks in reference to borrowings in Canada. I apprehend that he favours the people of Canada and the resources of Canada being called upon to give an equitable amount towards the present support of the war, and towards the diminution of that great borrowed sum that shall remain as a burden on our successors; but he seems to think that the loan which the Minister of Finance took from the people during the last few months was not advisable for two reasons: in the first place, because it perhaps went so far as to diminish the resources of the country which are required for carrying on our normal and present current business, and in the second place, because it was not a popular loan, and therefore took rather from those possessed of accumulated funds than from the general savings of the less wealthy classes. My hon. friend is scarcely correct in his views. If he will-look into the particulars of that loan he will find that there were 25,000 subscribers, which is a very large percentage of the population of Capada. Another fact he will find is that jf the original limit of the loan had been adhered to, the banks and the insurance companies, and the other large accumulators of the deposits of the people, would not have received a single scrip, because the loan would have all gone into the hands of the smaller investors. He will also find that of the $100,000,000 that were ultimately accepted, $75,000,000 came from the lesser investors and only $25,000,000 from the banks, the insurance companies, and the larger investors of accumulated funds. I think the desires of my hon. friend have really been met in that loan, and if not in that loan, they are met in the provision of the proposed legislation for the issue of debentures, in small sums, in order that the person who has one hundred dollars saved out of his earnings can put it into the war fund and thus help to carry on the activities of the war, and, at the same time, make an investment for himself which will bring a fair interest return. The prosecution of this plan with energy and discretion, throughout the length and breadth of Canada I regard as being an eminently fair way, and I hope it will prove a successful way, of interesting the people of small sav-
ings to take their part in the support of the war and at the same time to make wise provision for their own future.
My hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) then spoke of the tabulation of expenditures. He believes that as the expenditures all come out of the one pocket, and all go to the carrying on of the affairs of the country through the different branches of administration, it is simply vexatious and unnecessary, and perhaps misleading as well, if all are not grouped under one head. If this were done, he says, we should have no disr putes about surpluses and deficits. Well, I imagine that there was a reason why, in the denomination of expeditures in our early history, a system was inaugurated which made a distinction between capital expenditure and ordinary expenditure. This was a young country, with almost unlimited area, but with very sparse population. It was agreed on all hands that the men of the existing generation were not able to bear the burden of all the expense of opening up the country, and that posterity, which would enjoy the improvements that were made, might well be called upon to pay their proportion of the expense of making these improvements. The effect was to show a little in detail and to keep before the people what I do not think	is	a very
bad thing looked at in that light-that there are differences of expenditure, that some expenditures are for the present day and others -are for the future, and that it was fair and desirable th-at it should be known how these were distributed. Let us look at the war expenditure for example. The people of the future will read our public accounts, and they will find under our method of summation that in the years 1914, 1915, 1916-maybe 1917, we do not know-there was a vast increase in expenditure that the expenditure ran up from tens of millions of dollars to hundreds of millions of dollars, making, in the aggregate, many hundreds of millions. If / there were but one summation of expenditure, the men of the future would scarcely know how to rate and judge the people of these three or four years in their expenditure of these extraordinary sums. I think it eminently fair to have such a summation of expenditures as shall show that in these years a sparsely populated country tackled the problem of defence of liberty and justice for themselves and for the Empire, and that the interests of posterity justified the expenditure of these hundreds of millions of dollars and the

entering of that expenditure as a capital charge upon the country. So far I am not disposed to quarrel with this distribution of expenditures under different heads. But I will tell you where the moth and the rust do corrupt in a distribution like that. You do not have always a well-defined line to guide you as to what is ordinary expenditure and what is capital expenditure. And, in the diversion and change from one, side to the other that has taken place in the history of our country many and many a time, you are led into error, and there is great temptation to keep the ordinary expenditure down by transferring to the side of capital expenditure, what ought, in right and in conscience, to be put down on the side of ordinary expenditure. I say that, so far as normal capital expenditure and ordinary expenditure are now concerned in this country, I, for my. own part, would welcome the merging of both into one. This country has passed through its main period of capital expenditure. It has passed through it with sparse population. It is now at a state of advancement where it might very well place in one column all its expenditure and so prevent our continual juggling and dispute as to surplus and expenditures, and proper surplus and improper surplus.
The hon. member (Mr. A. K. Maclean) went on to speak of the expenditure and debt. He says the expenditures go up and have been going up, that the debt is increasing and will increase. That is true, and if the debt increases the payments for interest must increase. But what would the hon. gentleman have? The people of this country have made their decision. There is no wavering in it from Pacific to Atlantic. There never was a case in which unanimity was more complete. The few small and discordant voi,ces that we hear now and then protesting, only serve to bring out the remarkable completeness of that unanimity, and to call it more prominently to attention. The people of this country are behind this war, and underneath this war and the prosecution of it. Expenditures may go up, debt may increase, interest expenditures may grow larger, yet it is the determination of our people to make this expenditure, to bear this burden, until victory is won and the cause for which we are fighting is triumphant. But there never was a time in the history of Canada; there never was a time in the history of any Administration, when the call came more clearly to those administering the affairs of the country to be careful in the matter of expenditures; to direct them properly and to administer them with absolute honesty; to be strong enough and brave enough to refuse unnecessary demands. When the trenches call for munitions' and supplies; when the blood of the country is flowing from its veins in the struggle to preserve its ideals and its liberties; when those who are at home are contributing with generous self-sacrifice, and without murmur or repining, I say that to me as a member of the Government, to you as supporters of the Government, and to you gentlemen opposite, as a part of the great body which represents the people of this Dominion, the call comes to cut off every unnecessary expenditure, to refuse every unnecessary demand. It is our business to administer the funds of the people with perfect economy and to devote ourselves in so far as human beings are capable of doing it, to the sole purpose of prosecuting this war to its successful and final conclusion.
At six o'clock, the House took recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) made some observations by way of criticism in respect to charges made by the different departments to war account. He thought that, in the case of small amounts, that practice was " small potatoes " so to speak, and that in the case of larger amounts it should be charged up to the different departments. What is desirable, it seems to me, if we are going to put war expenditure in a column by itself, is that we should know our total war expenditure, so that we may realize exactly what the country has to bear on account of it.
